title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive from an automated license plate reader that was acted on as though it were an identification. The system matched a plate to a similar stolen vehicle after misreading its first letter, and the alert moved from a database into a roadside stop, where the driver was detained at gunpoint. The failure sits at the handoff between a machine-generated alert and a human decision to enforce.

Catching it would have required the check that Flock says its alerts already call for, an independent confirmation of the plate or the vehicle before the stop escalated. A single misread character is the kind of error a second look at the physical plate, or at the vehicle description attached to the stolen-vehicle record, would surface. The system was doing what it was built to do, which is flag a possible match, and the gap was in what happened after the flag.

What is not established is whether any such confirmation occurred before the detention, and the sheriff's attribution of the error to an illegal tinted plate cover is the agency's explanation rather than a finding about the reader's accuracy.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, 42, of York County, South Carolina, was reportedly detained at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter on his plate and linked his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later attributed the error to an illegal tinted plate cover and deemed the deputy’s conduct reasonable. Flock stated that alerts require independent confirmation before enforcement action.
